steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on learning DAG structure from dynamic graphs (GraphNOTEARS): background on Bayesian networks and DAG learning, why IID and static-graph methods fall short when graph data has temporal interactions, the challenges, our method, and our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Bayesian networks, DAGs and DAG structure learning
- Existing work: IID tabular data, static graph data
- Motivation: temporal information in graph data
- Two challenges of learning DAGs from dynamic graphs
- Our method: GraphNOTEARS
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Bayesian networks, DAGs, structure learning
  - BN = probabilistic graphical model of variables + conditional dependencies; widely used in ML
  - structure = DAG; convenient, interpretable output needed in high-stake AI (healthcare, finance, autonomous driving)
  - edges = directed generation relationships between variables (e.g. features)
  - edges unknown from prior knowledge -> DAG structure learning from observed data
- Existing work
  - mostly tabular data: samples IID
  - real world: associations between samples; features of a sample influenced by others through links
  - pioneer works: constraint-based methods for static (equilibrium) graph data; test conditional independencies of entity attributes
- Motivation: temporal info
  - Fig. 1: Bob's friends Lisa and Mary eat seafood, post recommendations + meal duration at t-1; Bob sees it; with enough time at t, likely chooses seafood
  - Bob's meal type at t determined by current available time + social recommendation at previous timestamp
  - COVID-19: infection risk from current protection (mask, social distance) + ratio of vaccinated/infected neighbors at previous timestamp two weeks ago
  - current methods ignore temporal interaction -> true generation process not revealed
- Two challenges
  - (1) what kind of DAG reflects feature generation in a dynamic graph? model generation of each new sample at each timestamp w/ time-lagged interaction
  - (2) how to learn the DAG efficiently from complex evolutional graph data? temporal + interaction info -> complicated mechanism; non-trivial
  - optimization techniques -> differentiable score function + blackbox solvers
- GraphNOTEARS
  - score-based, scales to dynamic graphs with high-dimensional node features
  - intra-slice matrix: contemporaneous relationships; inter-slice matrices: multi-step time-lagged graph influence
  - acyclicity constraint on whole graph
  - least-squares loss score function using temporal + interaction info and both structural matrices
  - smooth acyclicity constraint -> unconstrained augmented Lagrangian; standard second-order optimization
- Contributions
  - first to study DAG learning on dynamic graphs; reveal feature generation, BN skeletons, causal questions (interventions); explainable, robust, generalized algorithms
  - score-based method estimating structure + parameters of sparse DAG; arbitrary time-lagged order; no implicit assumptions on DAG topology
  - extensive simulations with broad settings; real-world datasets show rationality of inferred relationships

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
A Bayesian network (BN) is a probabilistic graphical model that represents a set of variables and the conditional dependencies between them. BNs have been used a lot in machine learning applications. The structure of a BN is a directed acyclic graph (DAG), and it gives a convenient and interpretable output, which is something that today's high-stake applications of artificial intelligence need, for example healthcare, finance and autonomous driving. The edges in a DAG represent the directed generation relationships between the variables (e.g., features) in a system. When we do not know these edges from prior knowledge, one possible solution is DAG structure learning, which means learning the edges of a graphical model from the observed data.

Most existing approaches for DAG learning work on tabular data, where each sample is drawn independently from the same distribution (IID data). But in real-world scenarios there are usually associations between samples, so the generation of the features of some samples may be influenced by other samples through the links between them. Some pioneer works proposed constraint-based methods to learn DAGs from static (i.e., equilibrium) graph data. These methods usually test the conditional independencies of the attributes of entities in the graph data to build DAGs among the variables.

But in many real-world scenarios the graph data has temporal information. For example, in Fig. 1, Bob's friends Lisa and Mary went to eat seafood, and at timestamp t-1 they posted recommendations and the duration of the meal on social media. Bob saw this information. When he has enough available time at timestamp t, he will very likely choose to eat seafood. So the value of Bob's meal type at timestamp t is determined both by the time he has available now and by the recommendation from his social network at the previous timestamp. Another example is COVID-19: the risk of a person being infected may be determined both by their current protection status (e.g., wearing a mask or keeping social distance) and by the ratio of their neighborhood who were vaccinated or infected at the previous timestamp two weeks ago. The current methods mostly ignore modeling this temporal interaction, so they cannot reveal the true data generation process accurately.

- Two challenges
  - (1) what kind of DAG reflects feature generation in a dynamic graph? model generation of each new sample at each timestamp w/ time-lagged interaction
  - (2) how to learn the DAG efficiently from complex evolutional graph data? temporal + interaction info -> complicated mechanism; non-trivial
  - optimization techniques -> differentiable score function + blackbox solvers
- GraphNOTEARS
  - score-based, scales to dynamic graphs with high-dimensional node features
  - intra-slice matrix: contemporaneous relationships; inter-slice matrices: multi-step time-lagged graph influence
  - acyclicity constraint on whole graph
  - least-squares loss score function using temporal + interaction info and both structural matrices
  - smooth acyclicity constraint -> unconstrained augmented Lagrangian; standard second-order optimization
- Contributions
  - first to study DAG learning on dynamic graphs; reveal feature generation, BN skeletons, causal questions (interventions); explainable, robust, generalized algorithms
  - score-based method estimating structure + parameters of sparse DAG; arbitrary time-lagged order; no implicit assumptions on DAG topology
  - extensive simulations with broad settings; real-world datasets show rationality of inferred relationships

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
A Bayesian network (BN) is a probabilistic graphical model that represents a set of variables and the conditional dependencies between them. BNs have been used a lot in machine learning applications. The structure of a BN is a directed acyclic graph (DAG), and it gives a convenient and interpretable output, which is something that today's high-stake applications of artificial intelligence need, for example healthcare, finance and autonomous driving. The edges in a DAG represent the directed generation relationships between the variables (e.g., features) in a system. When we do not know these edges from prior knowledge, one possible solution is DAG structure learning, which means learning the edges of a graphical model from the observed data.

Most existing approaches for DAG learning work on tabular data, where each sample is drawn independently from the same distribution (IID data). But in real-world scenarios there are usually associations between samples, so the generation of the features of some samples may be influenced by other samples through the links between them. Some pioneer works proposed constraint-based methods to learn DAGs from static (i.e., equilibrium) graph data. These methods usually test the conditional independencies of the attributes of entities in the graph data to build DAGs among the variables.

But in many real-world scenarios the graph data has temporal information. For example, in Fig. 1, Bob's friends Lisa and Mary went to eat seafood, and at timestamp t-1 they posted recommendations and the duration of the meal on social media. Bob saw this information. When he has enough available time at timestamp t, he will very likely choose to eat seafood. So the value of Bob's meal type at timestamp t is determined both by the time he has available now and by the recommendation from his social network at the previous timestamp. Another example is COVID-19: the risk of a person being infected may be determined both by their current protection status (e.g., wearing a mask or keeping social distance) and by the ratio of their neighborhood who were vaccinated or infected at the previous timestamp two weeks ago. The current methods mostly ignore modeling this temporal interaction, so they cannot reveal the true data generation process accurately.

There are two hard challenges when we learn DAGs from dynamic graphs. The first one is that a dynamic graph has complex temporal interactions between samples, so what kind of DAG would reflect the generation process of the features in a dynamic graph? Since the samples at each timestamp are generated based on the interactions from previous timestamps, the learned DAG should model how each new sample is generated at each timestamp, taking the time-lagged interaction information into account. The second one is how to learn a DAG efficiently from complex evolutional graph data. A dynamic graph has both temporal and interaction information, unlike IID data, so its data generation mechanism is more complicated, and designing a DAG learning method for dynamic graphs is non-trivial. Luckily, because optimization techniques are well developed, it is possible to build a differentiable score function that measures how valid candidate DAGs are and to use blackbox solvers to find the optimal DAG efficiently.

To address these two challenges, we propose GraphNOTEARS, an effective score-based approach for learning DAGs that can scale gracefully to dynamic graphs with high-dimensional node features. For the first challenge, we learn an intra-slice matrix to characterize contemporaneous relationships between variables, and several inter-slice matrices to characterize the multi-step time-lagged graph influence on the current timestamp. An acyclicity constraint is also needed so that the whole learned graph is acyclic. For the second challenge, we cast the problem as a score-based optimization problem and develop a score function based on a least-squares loss. The score function uses the temporal and interaction information, and the two kinds of learnable structural matrices, to reconstruct the data. With the smooth acyclicity constraint, we turn the original unsolvable constrained problem into an unconstrained augmented Lagrangian objective. This program can be solved efficiently with standard second-order optimization schemes. The main contributions of this paper are:

- To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to study the DAG learning problem on dynamic graphs. Dynamic graph data is everywhere in real applications, so learning DAGs on this data could reveal the underlying feature generation process, give skeletons for possible Bayesian networks, and answer causal questions, like the effect of different interventions. These applications are very important for building algorithms that are explainable, robust, and generalized.

- We develop a score-based learning method that estimates at the same time the structure and the parameters of a sparse DAG from a dynamic graph. The method can learn the relationships between variables of arbitrary time-lagged order in a dynamic graph, and it does not make any implicit assumptions about the topologies of the underlying DAG.

- We run extensive simulation experiments with a broad range of settings that may happen in the real world, and they validate that our approach is effective at revealing the feature generation mechanism of dynamic graphs. The experiments on real-world datasets show that the relationships inferred by GraphNOTEARS are rational.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
A Bayesian network (BN) is a probabilistic graphical model that represents a set of variables and their conditional dependencies. It has been widely used in machine learning applications [1,2,3]. The structure of a BN takes the form of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) and provides a convenient and interpretable output, which is needed in today's high-stake applications of artificial intelligence, such as healthcare, finance and autonomous driving. The edges in a DAG represent the directed generation relationships between variables (e.g., features) in a system. When these edges are not known from prior knowledge, one possible solution is DAG structure learning, namely, learning the edges in a graphical model from the observed data.

Existing approaches for DAG learning mostly focus on tabular data, i.e., each sample is independently drawn from the same distribution (IID data) [4,5,6,7,8]. However, in real-world scenarios there usually exist associations between samples, so the generation of features of certain samples may be influenced by other samples through the links between them. Several pioneer works have proposed constraint-based methods to learn DAGs from static (i.e., equilibrium) graph data [9,10,11]. They usually test the conditional independencies of the attributes of entities in graph data to form DAGs among those variables.

However, in many real-world scenarios graph data exhibits temporal information. For example, as shown in Fig. 1, Bob's friends, Lisa and Mary, went to eat seafood and posted recommendations and the duration of the meal on social media at timestamp t-1. Bob viewed this information. When he has enough available time at timestamp t, he will choose to eat seafood with high probability. Hence, the value of Bob's meal type at timestamp t is determined both by his current available time and by the recommendation from his social network at the previous timestamp. As another example, one's risk of being infected by COVID-19 may be determined both by current protection status (e.g., wearing a mask or keeping social distance) and by the ratio of the neighborhood who had been vaccinated or infected at the previous timestamp two weeks ago. Current methods largely ignore modeling such temporal interaction, so the true data generation process cannot be revealed accurately.

Learning DAGs from dynamic graphs poses two intractable challenges. First, a dynamic graph contains complex temporal interactions between samples, so what kind of DAG would reflect the generation process of features in a dynamic graph? As the samples at each timestamp are generated based on the interactions from previous timestamps, the learned DAG should model the generation process of each new sample at each timestamp, considering the time-lagged interaction information. Second, how can a DAG be learned efficiently from complex evolutional graph data? Compared with IID data, a dynamic graph contains both temporal and interaction information and hence has a more complicated data generation mechanism, so designing a DAG learning method for dynamic graphs is non-trivial. Fortunately, owing to well-developed optimization techniques, it is possible to develop a differentiable score function that measures the validity of candidate DAGs and to use blackbox solvers to find the optimal DAG efficiently.

To address these two challenges, we propose GraphNOTEARS, an effective score-based approach for learning DAGs that scales gracefully to dynamic graphs with high-dimensional node features. To solve the first challenge, we learn an intra-slice matrix to characterize contemporaneous relationships between variables, and several inter-slice matrices to characterize multi-step time-lagged graph influence on the current timestamp. Meanwhile, an acyclicity constraint ensures the acyclicity of the whole learned graph. For the second challenge, we cast the problem as a score-based optimization problem and develop a least-squares loss based score function, which leverages the temporal and interaction information, as well as the two kinds of learnable structural matrices, to reconstruct the data. With the smooth acyclicity constraint, we translate the original unsolvable constrained problem into an unconstrained augmented Lagrangian objective, which can be solved efficiently by standard second-order optimization schemes. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

- To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to study the DAG learning problem on dynamic graphs. Because dynamic graph data is ubiquitous in real applications, learning DAGs on such data could reveal the underlying feature generation process, provide skeletons for possible Bayesian networks, and answer causal questions, like the effect of various interventions. These applications are very important for building explainable, robust, and generalized algorithms.

- We develop a score-based learning method for simultaneously estimating the structure and parameters of a sparse DAG from a dynamic graph. The method can learn the relationships between variables of arbitrary time-lagged order in a dynamic graph, without any implicit assumptions on the underlying DAG topologies.

- We conduct extensive simulation experiments with a broad range of settings that may be encountered in the real world, validating the effectiveness of our approach in revealing the feature generation mechanism of dynamic graphs. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the rationality of the relationships inferred by GraphNOTEARS.
